narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 52.4% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. Being in the bottom decile that year, compared with an average around the middle of the class among accepted students, signaled to the model a higher risk of struggling with the bar. Your first-year class ranking was the third most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure; you again placed in the lowest decile while successful applicants averaged near the middle.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction and was the second most influential piece of information. At 39, you scored above the 37.2 average of accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the impact of your two low class rankings.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT or enrolling in a bar-preparation program that targets students with similar profiles. These steps can demonstrate a clearer trajectory toward passing the bar on the next application cycle. (248 words)
